title: Why Team Members Sometimes Hear Negative Feedback as Positive
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Using a deliberately extreme example, this piece explains a counterintuitive phenomenon: a team member can receive genuinely harsh feedback and walk away feeling relieved, because their own expectations were even worse. The author's argument is that feedback is interpreted relative to expectation, not in absolute terms, so a leader's message can land as reassurance rather than correction if the recipient braced for something worse. The prescribed fix isn't to make feedback harsher, but to surface the recipient's own self-assessment and expectations before delivering the evaluation, so the leader can calibrate the message to close the actual gap rather than an assumed one.
points: Feedback is interpreted relative to the recipient's expectations, not in absolute terms — the same harsh words can register as relief if the person expected worse.
The counterintuitive fix explicitly rejected is making feedback harsher; the real fix is surfacing the recipient's self-assessment before delivering the evaluation.
Asking what the team member thinks went well and poorly first puts their expectations 'on the table,' letting the leader calibrate the message to the real gap.
quotes: Even though the leader believes they have been straightforward and unfiltered in their criticism, the team member does not receive the message as negative.
In many other instances, the fault sits with the team member who “hears” an entirely different message than the one designed to emphasize a negative evaluation.
Expectations have a tremendous influence on how people hear the positivity or negativity of evaluations and feedback.
The solution to this dilemma is NOT to make negative feedback as harsh as possible, but instead to explore what people expect before offering the evaluation.
Now they can adjust their message to fit the expectations rather than sow misinterpretation. So easy, and yet so clever.
